1b:["$","div",null,{"className":"lg:col-span-8","children":[["$","header",null,{"className":"mb-12","children":[["$","h1",null,{"className":"font-serif font-light text-5xl md:text-6xl text-navy mb-4 leading-tight","children":"Samuel Haynes"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"w-24 h-[2px] bg-gold"}]]}],["$","section",null,{"className":"prose prose-navy max-w-none","children":[["$","div",null,{"className":"relative mb-12","children":[["$","$L1a",null,{"ref":"$undefined","iconNode":[["path",{"d":"M16 3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v6a2 2 0 0 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 1 1 1v1a2 2 0 0 1-2 2 1 1 0 0 0-1 1v2a1 1 0 0 0 1 1 6 6 0 0 0 6-6V5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2z","key":"rib7q0"}],["path",{"d":"M5 3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v6a2 2 0 0 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 1 1 1v1a2 2 0 0 1-2 2 1 1 0 0 0-1 1v2a1 1 0 0 0 1 1 6 6 0 0 0 6-6V5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2z","key":"1ymkrd"}]],"className":"lucide-quote absolute -left-8 -top-8 h-16 w-16 text-gold/10 pointer-events-none"}],["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Biography"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed prose prose-navy max-w-none  prose-headings:font-serif prose-headings:font-bold prose-headings:text-navy  prose-h3:text-3xl prose-h3:mt-10 prose-h3:mb-4 prose-a:text-gold hover:prose-a:text-navy prose-a:transition-colors prose-img:rounded-md prose-img:shadow-md prose-img:mx-auto prose-img:border prose-img:border-gold/20 prose-blockquote:border-l-4 prose-blockquote:border-gold prose-blockquote:pl-8  prose-blockquote:italic prose-blockquote:text-navy/80 prose-blockquote:font-serif prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:ml-8 prose-blockquote:my-10 [&_blockquote_p::before]:hidden [&_blockquote_p::after]:hidden","children":[["$","h3","h3-0",{"children":"Introduction: The Nationalist Voice of Belize"}],"\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":["Samuel Alfred Haynes (1899–1971) stands as one of the most intellectually vibrant, politically fearless, and culturally foundational figures in the modern history of Belize [1]. A decorated soldier, militant civil rights activist, prolific Pan-Africanist journalist, and gifted lyricist, Haynes dedicated his life to dismantling colonial oppression and instilling a profound sense of dignity, liberty, and self-determination among Black people in British Honduras and across the global diaspora [2]. Operating during a turbulent epoch characterized by global war, racial violence, and colonial exploitation, Haynes emerged from the crucible of working-class Belize City to become a pivotal leader in the 1919 Ex-Servicemen's Riot—an event widely recognized by historians as the first major anti-colonial uprising in 20th-century Belize [3]. His militant advocacy soon drew the attention of legendary Jamaican Pan-Africanist ",["$","$L1c","a-0",{"slug":"marcus-garvey","href":"/profiles/marcus-garvey","children":"Marcus Garvey"}],", catapulting Haynes into the highest executive echelons of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) in the United States [4]. Yet, despite his international prominence as a civil rights leader and editor of the world-renowned ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Negro World"}]," newspaper, Haynes' most enduring and universally celebrated contribution to his homeland lies in his literary genius [5]. He is the immortal lyricist of 'Land of the Gods,' a stirring patriotic poem written in defiance of colonial subjugation that was later adapted under the leadership of ",["$","$L1c","a-1",{"slug":"george-cadle-price","href":"/profiles/george-cadle-price","children":"George Cadle Price"}]," to become 'Land of the Free'—the official national anthem of an independent Belize [6]. Through his words, activism, and visionary courage, Samuel Haynes provided the ideological and spiritual soundtrack for a nation fighting to claim its freedom."]}],"\n","$L1d","\n","$L1e","\n","$L1f","\n","$L20","\n","$L21","\n","$L22","\n","$L23","\n","$L24","\n","$L25","\n","$L26","\n","$L27","\n","$L28","\n","$L29","\n","$L2a","\n","$L2b","\n","$L2c","\n","$L2d","\n","$L2e","\n","$L2f","\n","$L30","\n","$L31","\n","$L32","\n","$L33","\n","$L34","\n","$L35"]}]]}],"$L36","$L37",false]}],"$L38"]}]
3a:I[54477,["/_next/static/chunks/2i9p3n79r-dbf.js","/_next/static/chunks/2z-jpqdx1wamk.js","/_next/static/chunks/14mrh2-p_w84d.js","/_next/static/chunks/2uyb8-0enc77-.js","/_next/static/chunks/2zpyn7ne_o0vv.js"],"default"]

1d:["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"Early Life in Colonial British Honduras"}]
1e:["$","p","p-1",{"children":"Samuel Alfred Haynes was born in 1899 in the British colony of British Honduras, growing up within the vibrant yet deeply impoverished working-class neighborhoods of Belize Town (now Belize City) [1]. At the turn of the century, British Honduras existed under a rigid colonial hierarchy dominated by a white merchant elite and foreign forestry conglomerates who controlled the colony's land, mahogany trade, and political institutions [3]. The majority non-white population faced disenfranchisement, economic marginalization, and systemic racial discrimination [2]. Despite these oppressive socio-economic barriers, young Haynes exhibited an exceptional command of language, an acute intellect, and a voracious appetite for literature and history [4]. Educated in local colonial schools, he quickly perceived the stark contradictions between the British ideals of liberty taught in the classroom and the daily subjugation experienced by Belizean laborers [1]."}]
1f:["$","p","p-2",{"children":"As a young man coming of age amidst the intellectual currents of the early 1900s, Haynes was deeply influenced by the struggles of the working class and the emerging cultural consciousness within the Caribbean. He developed a deep reverence for the natural beauty of his homeland—its barrier reef, pristine rivers, and dense mahogany forests—while simultaneously harboring a burning indignation toward the colonial structures that denied his people the rights to the wealth beneath their feet [6]. This duality of immense patriotic love for the land and fierce resistance against colonial rule would become the defining hallmark of his entire philosophical and literary trajectory."}]
20:["$","p","p-3",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/12/Marcus_Garvey_1924-08-05.jpg","alt":"Historical portrait of Marcus Garvey (1924), the legendary Pan-African leader who recognized Samuel Haynes' brilliance and recruited him to lead the UNIA in the United States."}]}]
21:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":"World War I Service with the British West Indies Regiment"}]
22:["$","p","p-4",{"children":"With the outbreak of the First World War in 1914, the British Empire called upon its colonial subjects across the Caribbean to defend King and Country [1]. Driven by a complex mixture of youthful idealism, economic necessity, and the promise that military service would earn political respect and equal citizenship for West Indians, Samuel Haynes enlisted in the British Army in 1916 [7]. He was assigned to the British West Indies Regiment (BWIR), joining hundreds of fellow Belizean and West Indian volunteers on the arduous journey across the Atlantic [3]. Haynes served with distinction in the grueling Middle Eastern theatre, participating in military campaigns against the Ottoman Empire in Egypt, Palestine, and Mesopotamia [1]."}]
23:["$","p","p-5",{"children":"However, the reality of military service proved to be a bitter, disillusioning awakening for Haynes and his compatriots [3]. Rather than being treated as honorable brothers-in-arms, Black soldiers of the BWIR were subjected to virulent racism by British commanders [7]. They were frequently segregated, issued inferior rations, denied commissions as officers, and relegated to hazardous, menial labor tasks such as digging trenches, hauling heavy ammunition under enemy artillery fire, and clearing sanitation ditches [3]. When West Indian soldiers dared to protest these indignities, they were met with draconian military discipline [7]. For Haynes, witnessing the shedding of Black blood for an empire that viewed them as racially inferior shattered any lingering illusions of benevolent colonial benevolence [1]. The battlefield became his ideological crucible, transforming the educated young soldier into a radical, militant anti-colonial nationalist determined to fight for self-determination upon his return home."}]
24:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"'Samuel Haynes transformed the bitter disillusionment of Black West Indian veterans into a powerful beacon of anti-colonial nationalism, giving voice to a burgeoning Belizean identity through organizational leadership and immortal verse.'"}],"\n"]}]
25:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"The 1919 Ex-Servicemen's Riot and Awakening of Anti-Colonialism"}]
26:["$","p","p-6",{"children":"In 1919, Samuel Haynes and his fellow surviving veterans returned to British Honduras expecting welcoming heroes' receptions and promised employment opportunities [3]. Instead, they stepped off the troopships into a colony gripped by severe economic recession, exorbitant inflation, food shortages, and widespread racial hostility from colonial administrators [7]. Compounding their grievance, colonial officials refused to grant the returning veterans their promised military pensions and back pay, while local white merchants artificially inflated the prices of basic foodstuffs [3]."}]
39:T537,The simmering fury boiled over on the night of July 22, 1919, when hundreds of exasperated ex-servicemen marched through the streets of Belize Town in what erupted into the historic 1919 Ex-Servicemen's Riot [1]. The uprising quickly gained massive popular support from the urban working class, targeting colonial businesses, government buildings, and oppressive merchant establishments [3]. Samuel Haynes emerged as a primary intellectual and strategic leader during the revolt [7]. While sharing the justifiable anger of the veterans, Haynes also demonstrated extraordinary maturity and tactical foresight [1]. Once the initial demonstration made its powerful statement against colonial oppression, Haynes used his commanding respect among the troops to help restore civil order, preventing unnecessary loss of life while channeling the movement's energy into organized political demands [7]. In the aftermath of the uprising, when colonial authorities cracked down and imprisoned several veteran leaders, Haynes spearheaded public agitation and legal defense efforts, ultimately securing pardons and concessions from the colonial governor [1]. The 1919 uprising permanently altered the political landscape of Belize, marking the birth of modern Belizean labor consciousness and setting the stage for future nationalist leaders like 27:["$","p","p-7",{"children":["$39",["$","$L1c","a-0",{"slug":"antonio-soberanis-gomez","href":"/profiles/antonio-soberanis-gomez","children":"Antonio Soberanis Gómez"}]," and ",["$","$L1c","a-1",{"slug":"philip-goldson","href":"/profiles/philip-goldson","children":"Philip Goldson"}],"."]}]
28:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"Leadership in Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA)"}]
29:["$","p","p-8",{"children":["Recognizing that local agitation needed global solidarity, Samuel Haynes channeled the momentum of the 1919 veterans' movement into organizing the British Honduras division of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) [4]. Founded by the brilliant Jamaican visionary ",["$","$L1c","a-0",{"slug":"marcus-garvey","href":"/profiles/marcus-garvey","children":"Marcus Garvey"}],", the UNIA preached racial pride, Black economic independence, Pan-African unity, and anti-colonial self-reliance [2]. Haynes became the general secretary and intellectual dynamo of the local Belize City branch, which quickly swelled to become one of the most active and influential UNIA chapters in the entire Caribbean, boasting thousands of dedicated members [4]. Working closely with prominent local organizers such as nurse ",["$","$L1c","a-1",{"slug":"vivian-seay","href":"/profiles/vivian-seay","children":"Vivian Seay"}],", Haynes established local UNIA businesses, educational cooperatives, and mutual aid societies that empowered the Belizean working class [3]."]}]
2a:["$","p","p-9",{"children":["In July 1921, Haynes orchestrated a historic triumph by successfully inviting ",["$","$L1c","a-0",{"slug":"marcus-garvey","href":"/profiles/marcus-garvey","children":"Marcus Garvey"}]," himself to visit British Honduras [4]. Garvey's arrival in Belize City was met with ecstatic jubilation by thousands of citizens [3]. During his stay, Garvey recognized the extraordinary oratorical brilliance, organizational genius, and ideological clarity of young Samuel Haynes [1]. Impressed by his leadership, Garvey personally recruited Haynes to relocate to the United States to assume executive leadership responsibilities within the global UNIA headquarters [5]. Accepting the call to advance the international Black liberation struggle, Haynes migrated to America in the early 1920s, embarking on a brilliant career on the world stage [4]."]}]
2b:["$","blockquote","blockquote-1",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"'O, Land of the Free by the Carib Sea, / Our manhood we pledge to thy liberty! / No tyrants here linger, despots must flee / This tranquil haven of democracy.'"}],"\n"]}]
2c:["$","p","p-10",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e7/Flag_of_British_Honduras_%281919%E2%80%931981%29.svg","alt":"Historical Flag of British Honduras (1919–1981). Samuel Haynes penned his immortal anthem during this colonial era to awaken Belizean national pride and demand an end to foreign subjugation."}]}]
2d:["$","h3","h3-5",{"children":"Journalistic Contributions: Editing the Negro World in the United States"}]
2e:["$","p","p-11",{"children":["Upon arriving in the United States, Samuel Haynes rose rapidly through the national ranks of the UNIA [1]. He was elected President of the influential Pittsburgh Division of the UNIA, where he mobilized thousands of African American steelworkers and Caribbean immigrants, championing civil rights, labor equity, and Black entrepreneurship across the industrial Midwest [5]. His leadership caught the attention of the global movement's intellectual elite, leading to his appointment to the editorial board of the ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Negro World"}],"—the official global newspaper of the UNIA [4]."]}]
2f:["$","p","p-12",{"children":["With a weekly circulation reaching hundreds of thousands of readers across the Americas, Europe, and Africa, the ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Negro World"}]," was the most widely read and influential Black newspaper on the planet [5]. As an editor and contributing writer, Haynes utilized his sharp, eloquent pen to denounce European colonialism in Africa and the Caribbean, expose racial lynching and segregation in the Jim Crow South, and advocate for international human rights [1]. His journalistic essays were celebrated for their analytical rigor and passionate defense of Black dignity [4]. Even while operating in the United States, Haynes never forgot his native Belize; he regularly published articles detailing the economic exploitation of British Honduras, keeping the struggles of the Belizean working class visible before an international audience [3]."]}]
30:["$","h3","h3-6",{"children":"'Land of the Gods': Composition of the Immortal Anthem"}]
31:["$","p","p-13",{"children":"Despite his international travels and global activism, Samuel Haynes’ heart remained inextricably tethered to his beloved Belize [1]. During the late 1920s, while reflecting deeply on the natural splendor, cultural resilience, and unrealized destiny of his homeland, Haynes penned a masterful poetic ode originally titled 'Land of the Gods' [6]. Written during an era when Belizeans were forced to sing 'God Save the King' and pledge allegiance to a distant British monarch, Haynes' poem was a revolutionary act of cultural reclamation [4]."}]
32:["$","p","p-14",{"children":["The lyrics painted a breathtaking panorama of Belize's physical geography—its Baymen heritage, the sparkling Caribbean Sea, the fertile river valleys, and the majestic forest canopy—while embedding a profound political philosophy of freedom, democracy, and resistance against tyranny [6]. Lines such as ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"'No tyrants here linger, despots must flee / This tranquil haven of democracy'"}]," were direct rebukes of colonial despotism and a rallying cry for self-determination [4]. Recognizing the emotional power of Haynes' verse, prominent Belizean musical director and composer Selwyn Walford Young composed a majestic, stirring musical score to accompany the poem in 1963 [6]. Together, Haynes' words and Young's music created an anthem that immediately captivated the hearts of the Belizean people, becoming the unofficial patriotic hymn of the nationalist movement [1]."]}]
33:["$","h3","h3-7",{"children":"Adaptation to 'Land of the Free' and National Legacy"}]
34:["$","p","p-15",{"children":["As British Honduras accelerated along the path toward peaceful decolonization under the leadership of Premier ",["$","$L1c","a-0",{"slug":"george-cadle-price","href":"/profiles/george-cadle-price","children":"George Cadle Price"}]," and the People's United Party during the 1960s and 1970s, the quest for authentic national symbols took center stage [6]. Price and the nationalist leadership recognized that Samuel Haynes' 'Land of the Gods' perfectly encapsulated the soul and aspirations of the emerging nation [1]. With slight modifications to adapt the phrasing for modern independence—most notably retitling the work 'Land of the Free'—the song was officially adopted as the national anthem of Belize upon the attainment of sovereign independence on September 21, 1981 [6]."]}]
35:["$","p","p-16",{"children":"Although Samuel Haynes passed away in 1971 before witnessing the official lowering of the Union Jack and the raising of the Belizean flag, his spirit lives on every time his anthem is sung across the nation [1]. Today, he is revered as a national hero of Belize [2]. In posthumous recognition of his monumental life's work, the Belizean government and community leaders established the Samuel Haynes Institute of Excellence in Belize City—a premier educational and community development center dedicated to uplifting young Belizeans through academic support, arts, and leadership training [8]. From the trenches of World War I to the executive suites of the UNIA and the eternal verses of the national anthem, Samuel Haynes dedicated his entire existence to the liberation of his people, bequeathing to Belize a legacy of freedom that will endure forever."}]
36:["$","$L3a",null,{"title":"Learn about the legacy of Samuel Haynes","url":"https://caribbeanlegacyarchive.com/profiles/samuel-haynes"}]
3b:T58c,Samuel Alfred Haynes was a pioneering Belizean nationalist, military veteran, civil rights leader, and prolific lyricist whose work played a foundational role in shaping modern Belizean national identity. As a veteran of the British West Indies Regiment in World War I, he became a key organizer and leader of the landmark 1919 Ex-Servicemen's Riot in Belize City, protesting racial discrimination and economic injustice. He subsequently co-founded and led the British Honduras branch of [Marcus Garvey](/profiles/marcus-garvey)'s Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA), empowering the working class through self-reliance programs and facilitating Garvey’s historic 1921 visit to Belize.

Recruited by Garvey to the United States, Haynes served as President of the UNIA’s Pittsburgh Division and gained international prominence as an editor and writer for the world-renowned *Negro World* newspaper, championing global anti-colonialism and civil rights. His most enduring national contribution is his composition of the patriotic poem 'Land of the Gods,' set to music by Selwyn Walford Young. Adapted under the leadership of [George Cadle Price](/profiles/george-cadle-price) as 'Land of the Free,' it was adopted as the official national anthem of sovereign Belize in 1981. His legacy of excellence and community empowerment is commemorated today by the Samuel Haynes Institute of Excellence in Belize City.37:["$","div",null,{"className":"mb-12 pt-12 border-t border-gold/10","children":[["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Major Contributions"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed bg-white p-8 border-l-4 border-tropical-green shadow-sm","children":"$3b"}]]}]
